scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Tsakonikos originates from Tsakonia, a mountainous region situated largely within Arcadia in the Peloponnese peninsula of Greece.

According to local legend, the winding pattern of the dance is connected to ancient mythology, specifically referencing the Crane dance (Geranos) performed by Theseus after escaping the Labyrinth of King Minos, or Apollo's slaying of the Python at Delphi.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Tsakonikos serves as both a communal celebration and a cultural identifier for the Tsakonian-speaking community of the Peloponnese.
The symbolic winding of the serpentine line carries associations with survival, navigation through complex paths, and historical mythology surrounding the ancient Cretan Labyrinth.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance takes place in an open circle, executed to an asymmetrical 5/4 meter broken into a 3+2 count structure.
Dancers link arms closely in an elbow hold called 'angaze' (αγκαζέ), maintaining their hands held up high.

The movement path follows a slow, continuous winding progression: the leader guides the head of the circle inward so that the open line winds upon itself into a tight, snail-shaped spiral before reversing or uncoiling the pattern.
Watch for Snail spiral winding.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In traditional village settings like Ayios Andreas, the dance is executed outdoors during communal gatherings and festival celebrations.
Dancers wear traditional regional Greek attire, historically featuring white shirts ('aspra poukamisa') that are specifically mentioned within the song texts linked to the performance.
The high elbow-hold arm positioning ensures that dancers maintain a unified physical structure while navigating the winding path.
